terms.grammar: cedo, old imperative “give here”, with the accusative
evidence: Plaut. Most. 332: Cedo manum, nōlō equidem tē adflīgī.
Plaut. Capt. 859: Cedo manum. — Em manum.
terms.comment: Latin asks for the hand rather than telling the child to hold it; the answer is Em manum or Em tenē, “here, hold on”. Cedo is not cēdō, “give way”; see give it here.

evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 87: manum dā et sequere
Quint. 2.3.7: det manum et gradum suum minuat

phrases.english: Hold my hand; we’re crossing the road.

phrases.latin: Cedo manum, nōlō equidem tē adflīgī. — Em tenē. — Age, ī simul.
phrases.english: Give me your hand, I don’t want you to fall. — Here, hold on. — Come on, walk with me.

phrases.latin: ut vēlōcissimus quoque, sī forte iter cum parvolō faciat, det manum et gradum suum minuat
phrases.english: as even the fastest walker, if he happens to be on the road with a little child, gives him his hand and shortens his stride

sources: Lewis & Short: cedo · Lewis & Short: manus
